body_markdown:
Wales introduces a new NHS waiting list plan aimed at reducing long delays, increasing surgical capacity and changing how follow-up appointments are managed.


Wales is introducing a major new strategy aimed at reducing NHS waiting lists, improving access to treatment and tackling the growing number of patients waiting for hospital care.


One of the biggest changes under the new plan is that patients will no longer automatically receive routine follow-up appointments after treatment. Instead, further appointments are expected to be arranged when healthcare professionals believe they are clinically necessary.


The Welsh government hopes this change will release tens of thousands of hospital appointment slots and allow consultants to spend more time treating patients who are waiting for their first specialist assessment.


The plan also places greater emphasis on treating people who have been waiting the longest. However, doctors will still be able to prioritise other patients when there is a clear medical reason to do so.


## Welsh NHS Waiting Lists Remain Under Pressure


The new strategy comes as NHS waiting lists in Wales continue to face significant pressure.


The latest figures referenced in the announcement showed that more than **698,500 cases were on NHS waiting lists in Wales in June** . Nearly 4,100 cases involved people who had already been waiting for at least two years.


That figure represents an increase compared with earlier in the year, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing the Welsh NHS.


The Welsh government has previously said that two-year waits for planned treatment should be eliminated within months. However, the latest strategy does not provide a specific deadline for achieving that target.


Instead, the government has set a broader ambition of reducing the overall waiting list to approximately **460,000 cases** , which is around the level seen before the Covid-19 pandemic, by the end of the current Senedd term.


Further information about specific deadlines and implementation is expected to be provided later in the year.


## Why Are Follow-Up Appointments Being Changed?


A key part of the new Wales NHS waiting list plan is to make better use of existing hospital capacity.


At present, a significant amount of NHS capacity is used for follow-up appointments. More than one million cases are reportedly waiting for follow-up care in Wales.


The government's proposal is designed to reduce unnecessary or routine follow-ups where a patient's clinical condition does not require another appointment.


Instead of automatically booking another consultation, healthcare teams would determine whether additional care, testing or monitoring is needed.


The intention is not to prevent patients from receiving necessary medical attention. Rather, the government says the approach is designed to ensure hospital resources are focused on patients who need specialist assessment or treatment.


## More Time for New Patients and Surgery


The plan also aims to change how consultants divide their working time.


Under the proposed model, doctors are expected to spend a larger proportion of their clinical time seeing new patients.


The government wants around 70% of consultant clinic time to be focused on new patients, compared with approximately 30% currently.


Surgical services are also expected to undergo changes. The plan proposes increasing the proportion of consultant time dedicated to operating, with a target of approximately 80% spent in theatres and 20% in clinics in relevant specialties.


If achieved, the changes could increase the number of patients receiving operations while reducing the amount of time people spend waiting for their first specialist appointment.


## Additional NHS Investment Announced


The waiting list strategy is supported by **£145 million of funding** .


The investment includes money for maintaining and upgrading equipment, developing new surgical facilities and increasing day-to-day NHS activity.


Around £20 million is earmarked for maintenance and equipment, while £25 million is intended to support the development of new surgical hubs.


A further £100 million will be used to increase NHS activity and help services treat more patients.


The government believes that expanding capacity within the existing NHS could provide a more sustainable solution than relying heavily on temporary measures.


## Surgical Hubs and Weekend Treatment


Increasing surgical capacity is another important element of the strategy.


The government plans to expand surgical activity, including weekend operations, particularly in specialties where patients have experienced the longest delays.


Treatment hubs are also part of the wider approach. Plaid Cymru has previously committed to developing as many as 10 treatment hubs across Wales.


These facilities could provide additional locations for planned procedures and help separate scheduled treatment from other pressures experienced by general hospitals.


The government hopes regional cooperation will also allow health boards to share successful approaches and make better use of available staff, facilities and equipment.


## Faster Referrals and Better Diagnosis


Reducing the NHS waiting list is not only about increasing the number of operations.


The new strategy also focuses on the early stages of a patient's healthcare journey.


GP referrals are expected to be reviewed more quickly so that patients can find out sooner whether they need further tests, investigations or specialist treatment.


The government also wants to increase diagnostic capacity and make greater use of digital technology.


Faster access to scans, tests and specialist assessments could help reduce the time between a GP referral and a confirmed diagnosis.


In turn, this could allow treatment to begin sooner for patients who require it.


## NHS Boards to Be Held Accountable


Another significant feature of the plan is how health boards will be funded and assessed.


Under the new approach, health boards are expected to demonstrate that treatments have actually been completed rather than simply promising to deliver certain levels of activity.


This is intended to create stronger accountability and ensure that additional government funding results in measurable improvements for patients.


Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor has described the strategy as a long-term change rather than another temporary attempt to reduce waiting lists.


The government says health boards will be expected to make permanent changes to how services operate.


## Healthcare Leaders Welcome the Direction, But Warn of Challenges


The Welsh NHS Confederation has welcomed several elements of the plan, including greater regional cooperation, additional diagnostic capacity, surgical hubs and changes to planned care.


However, healthcare leaders have also warned that NHS waiting lists cannot be considered separately from wider pressures affecting health and social care.


The NHS continues to face challenges involving staffing, demand, hospital capacity and pressure on other parts of the healthcare system.


This means that simply changing appointment arrangements may not be enough to solve the waiting list problem on its own.


Opposition parties have also questioned the government's lack of a precise deadline for eliminating two-year waits.


Critics argue that patients who have already spent years waiting need clear information about when they can realistically expect treatment.


## What Could the New NHS Plan Mean for Patients?


For patients, the changes could have both practical benefits and concerns.


If routine follow-up appointments can be safely reduced, consultants may have more time to see people waiting for their first appointment. Increased surgical capacity could also mean more operations being completed each week.


However, patients may want reassurance that reducing automatic follow-ups will not result in important symptoms or complications being overlooked.


Clinical decision-making will therefore remain crucial. The success of the plan is likely to depend on healthcare professionals being able to identify which patients require continued monitoring and which can safely be discharged from routine follow-up.


The Welsh government says the reforms will be led by clinicians and designed around patients rather than organisational structures.


## A Long-Term Test for the Welsh NHS


The new Wales NHS waiting list plan represents an attempt to address one of the country's most persistent healthcare challenges.


With hundreds of thousands of cases still waiting and thousands of patients facing waits of two years or more, the pressure on the health service remains substantial.


The government is betting that better use of existing NHS resources, additional investment, increased surgical capacity, faster diagnosis and fewer unnecessary follow-up appointments can make a lasting difference.


The coming months will be important in determining whether those changes translate into shorter waiting times.


For patients, the most important measure will ultimately be whether they can access diagnosis, specialist advice and treatment more quickly.

BBC News report published on **3 September 2026** , alongside statements and figures attributed to the Welsh Government, NHS organisations.
